summary: I (one-person team) created a simple machine learning algorithm that ranks how likely it is that a latitude/longitude location can demonstrate one of many possible types of vegetative topologies within the bounding box of California. The idea is that farmers may use the program to query what sorts of vegetative landscapes (environments or crops) are typical to their location, which in turn can inspire what kinds of crops would likely do well in their location.
details:
Although the application itself is quite rudimentary (a simple python script that runs a basic machine learning model), the intention was to demonstrate a machine learning algorithm that integrates with NASA-powered databases to provide information to farmers on what kinds of croplands/environments are typical of their location, with the idea being that it can be used anywhere with basic Internet access to give ideas for Californian farmers on might do well in their area. Python was the programming language used extensively (solely) in this project, specifically depending on pandas and numpy to index and do math over the datasets, pytorch to train the machine learning model produced for this project, and geocoder, osgeo, pyproj, and rasterio to index the .tif files used to acquire data for the model to train from. The project is intended to serve as a launchpad for more sophisticated tools to integrate with both NASA's databases, such as more sophisticated machine learning models or a more developed and user-friendly front end to use the model.

Considerations included what kinds of factors would the project's machine learning algorithm depend on to run, what kinds of data is easily accessible in the 2-day development cycle, and how can this be made to be as user-friendly and non-intrusive as possible for non-technical users.
